title: Evidence and sourcing
instruction: Name the kind of evidence behind each claim, with its source and any label beside it.

opener.caption: Connection L02 as our systems atlas records it. Each numeral marks a part that carries its evidence, and the list names the rule that sets it.

intro: Every chart, diagram and claim we publish carries its evidence: what kind it is, how strong, who published it and when. Our systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, grades each claim it holds from documented to hypothesis, and that evidence grade sets the words and lines a page may use.
Where chapter 01 or chapter 02 already states a rule, the rules here cite it and show how a figure keeps it.

groups.title: Kinds of evidence and their grades
groups.line: A title says what kind of evidence it rests on, and every word, line and mark about that evidence follows the grade our systems atlas gives it.

groups.title: Sources, dates and labels
groups.line: A reader can trace every number to its publisher and its date, and can tell what we invented from what we found.

groups.title: Records, quotes and corrections
groups.line: Dated events, quoted words and our own corrections each take a form a reader can check against the record.

rules.title: Title each chart or diagram as a finding, an association, an estimate or an illustration.
rule: An evidence label, a chip in the chart chip colors, sits above every chart title and names the kind of evidence in one of four words. A finding is a measured result with a source and a period, such as a count or a survey figure. An association is what our systems atlas defines as “Two measures that move together without an established causal path.” An estimate rests on a model’s assumptions, such as a projection. An illustration shows how a design works with invented values.

The grade follows the label in words: the atlas’s grade for a figure from the atlas (Rule 13.2), and Documented for an official statistic or a public record, with its source after the colon. A diagram of atlas connections prints the grade word of its least certain step in the label’s place.

text: A reader decides how far to trust a chart before reading it closely. The label names what they are looking at: something measured, a pattern, a projection or a demonstration. A title that states a cause over a chart of a pattern misleads with true numbers, and the label puts that difference in the first word on the figure.
why.basis: Design judgment, from the chart system our founder and editor approved in November 2026

correct.caption: Four chart heads, one of each kind, with the charts under them left out. The finding gives its margin of error, the association’s note says the pattern does not show cause, and the estimate’s note gives the method behind its number.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.1. The label says Finding and the title says concentrated hiring “cuts” wages, over a study that measured a pattern across job markets, so a reader takes the pattern for a cause.

specs.label: Evidence label
specs.value: Finding, Association, Estimate or Illustration, in the label style on the chart chip fill, which turns with the theme

specs.label: Grade line
specs.value: After the label: the atlas’s grade for an atlas figure; Documented for an official statistic or a public record, then its source, as in “Documented: a Census Bureau survey”

specs.label: A finding
specs.value: A count or a survey tabulation, with the publisher’s margin of error where one exists, at its stated confidence

specs.label: An estimate
specs.value: A figure that rests on a model’s assumptions, such as a projection, a small-area model or a with-and-without calculation, with its range or method

specs.label: An association
specs.value: Words such as “went with” at any grade, and a note that the pattern does not show cause

specs.label: An illustration
specs.value: Invented values only, with “Illustrative data” beside the chart (Rule 13.8)

specs.label: An atlas diagram
specs.value: The grade word of its least certain step in the label’s place, and what that grade belongs to after it

specs.label: Measure line
specs.value: The line under the title that says what is counted, in what unit, where and when

builders: Store the kind in the chart’s spec as its evidence field and print the label from that field, so the label and the title come from one record.
Take an atlas claim’s kind from its own words: a claim the atlas writes as “associated with” is an association, whatever its grade.

rules.title: Give the title the verb its evidence grade allows.
rule: House rule H08 in chapter 02 gives each evidence grade its verb: record words such as “passed” or “stood at” for documented, a direct verb such as “raises” for well supported, “can” or “may” for plausible, both readings at the same length for contested, and a label that marks a hypothesis as untested. A title takes the grade of the claim it states, read from the atlas record or set by Rule 13.1 for a figure from outside the atlas.

The atlas names each connection, a claimed causal link from one of its variables to another, and some names keep a direct verb at a lower grade, such as “Better public services build earned trust”, graded plausible. We print such a name in quotation marks after its typed chip, as the atlas writes it, and write our own title in the verb the grade allows.

text: The verb carries most of a title’s claim. “Raises” tells a reader that strong studies agree, while “can raise” says some evidence points that way, so a verb sized to the grade keeps the claim honest in the sentence a reader repeats. Rule 02.16 asks for the same verbs inside a sentence.

correct.caption: Five connections from our systems atlas, one at each grade, each titled with the verb its grade allows beside the record it states. The contested link takes both readings at 15 words each.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.2. The label says plausible, and the title states the link with the direct verb “build”, which only well-supported evidence allows.

specs.label: Documented
specs.value: Record words: passed, ruled, stood at, reported, had spent

specs.label: Well supported
specs.value: A direct verb: raises, lowers

specs.label: Plausible
specs.value: “Can” or “may”, once, with no other softener

specs.label: Contested
specs.value: Both readings at the same length (Rule 01.16)

specs.label: Hypothesis
specs.value: “Untested” in the title’s first words

specs.label: An atlas name
specs.value: In quotation marks after its chip, as the atlas writes it

specs.label: Where the grade comes from
specs.value: The atlas record the title states, read by script, or Rule 13.1 for an outside figure

builders: Read the grade from the record the title states and check the verb against H08’s table before the chart ships. A title about a whole loop takes the grade of its least certain step, read from the grades of its connections.

rules.title: Print the atlas’s grade words with a plain gloss, from one table.
rule: Our systems atlas stores its grades in several fields and spells some of them two ways: well-supported on a connection and well_supported on an issue record, plausible_contested on a connection and contested on a claim. Every page prints one display word for each grade, from the table in this rule, with a short gloss in a chart key and the atlas’s own definition the first time a page uses the word. A gloss is a plain phrase that says what the word means, such as “some evidence” for Plausible.

Two more words sit in the table. Mixed, for a claim whose parts point different ways, prints as the atlas words it, beside the record it describes. Retired marks an issue record the atlas no longer uses, which is a status, so it stays out of every grade key.

text: A reader who meets Well supported in a key and well_supported in a table has to wonder whether they mean the same thing. One table gives every page the same word for the same grade, and the gloss hands a newcomer the meaning without a trip to the atlas’s methods.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s methods and glossary; the display words and glosses are design judgment

correct.caption: The mapping table: every grade value our systems atlas holds on October 15, 2026, with its count, the word a page prints, the gloss a key prints and the line a connection draws.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.3. The key prints the atlas’s stored values, gives one grade two spellings and adds Strong, a word that matches no grade.

specs.label: Display words
specs.value: Documented, Well supported, Plausible, Contested, Hypothesis, in that order

specs.label: Key glosses
specs.value: On the public record; strong research evidence; some evidence; evidence disputed; not yet tested, as Rule 12.6’s key prints them

specs.label: First use
specs.value: The atlas glossary’s definition, quoted

specs.label: Contested
specs.value: The atlas’s plausible_contested and contested values, and its contested flag

specs.label: Outside the keys
specs.value: Mixed beside its record; Retired as a record status

builders: Map every grade through one function that reads this table, and stop the build on any value the table does not hold, so a new value in the atlas waits until the table names it.

rules.title: Draw a connection’s grade in the atlas’s line code.
rule: A connection, the arrow from one variable to another in our systems atlas, takes the line of its own grade, drawn by the atlas build’s own function as Rule 10.10 sets out: solid for documented and well supported, dashed for plausible, dash and dot for contested, and dots for a hypothesis. Its grade word prints beside it, and a documented connection’s label starts with the record square, a filled square that says the public record itself shows the link.

A loop, a chain of connections that returns to where it started, draws each step in its own line, so its least certain step stands out, and each step of a conceptual loop, one with no complete chain of numbered connections, draws as a hollow line. The oa.chart.grade tokens hold every number, listed in the Specifications.

text: Documented and well supported share the solid line, and the record square tells them apart in gray print or on a photocopy, where a key is easy to miss. Drawing each step at its own grade shows a reader where a loop is weakest before they read its record.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s line code, with the record square and the hollow line our founder and editor approved in October 2026

correct.caption: Four loops from our systems atlas, each step in the line of its grade with its word, under a label that gives the loop’s least certain grade. The record square marks Loop R10’s two documented steps, Loop R16 closes on an untested step, and Loop B2’s step is hollow because the atlas gives it no numbered connection.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.4. Every step of Loop R10 is solid and none carries its grade, so the plausible step the atlas calls its weakest looks as firm as the documented ones.

specs.label: Documented and Well supported
specs.value: Solid

specs.label: Plausible
specs.value: Dashed, 4 and 2 line widths, butt caps: 8 and 4 px on a 2 px line

specs.label: Contested
specs.value: Dash and dot, 4, 1.5, 1 and 1.5 line widths: 8, 3, 2 and 3 px on a 2 px line

specs.label: Hypothesis
specs.value: Round dots 2.5 line widths apart, 5 px on a 2 px line, stopping 1.5 line widths short of the arrowhead

specs.label: Widths and fit
specs.value: Lines at 2, 3 or 6 px; each pattern stretched to start and end on ink

specs.label: Hollow line
specs.value: Two 1 px rails, 1 line width apart: 4 px across on a 2 px line

specs.label: Shortest run
specs.value: 20 line widths, 40 px on a 2 px line, key samples included; a shorter step prints its grade in words beside it

specs.label: Record square
specs.value: 7 px, filled in the label’s ink, inline before the word Documented and nowhere else

specs.label: Beside the event mark
specs.value: An event’s shape sits only at the head of an event row, with the figure’s key (Rule 13.11)

builders: Take each step’s grade from its own connection record and draw the line with the atlas build’s wire_marks, so the pattern fits the line’s length and starts and ends on ink. Read every number from the oa.chart.grade tokens.

rules.title: Keep grade, effect size, uncertainty and delay apart, each with its own mark.
rule: Four properties of a claim keep their own marks and words. The evidence grade takes the line of Rule 13.4 or the grade word. A reform’s effect size prints as the atlas’s ordinal code, a rank of small, moderate or large with no measured amount, in one row for each outcome family, one of the four groups of results the atlas judges reforms by. Uncertainty prints in the atlas’s own words, or for a survey figure as its margin of error, the range around the figure that sampling allows. Delay, the time an effect takes, draws as ticks on the connection.

No mark carries two properties, and the four outcome families never add into one score. Our systems atlas gives the reason: “The four outcome families use different units. A reform can improve one while imposing a cost on another, and the evidence behind each estimate differs in quality.”

text: Each property answers its own question: how strong the evidence is, how large the change, how sure the atlas is of that size, and how soon it comes. A mark that carries two at once, such as a thicker line for stronger evidence, lets a large effect on thin evidence pass for a small one on strong evidence.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s methods and outcomes, with the effect and delay marks our founder and editor approved in October 2026

correct.caption: Reform R-30 with each property in its own place: the grade of the evidence that it works in the label, its effect on each outcome family with the atlas’s qualifiers kept, the atlas’s confidence in its own words, and the delay of each connection it targets, marked in Rule 12.5’s red.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.5. The card adds four codes into one score of +5, draws the grade as a bar’s thickness and leaves the delay out.

specs.label: Grade
specs.value: The line of Rule 13.4, or the grade word

specs.label: Effect size
specs.value: The atlas’s code and words, one row per outcome family: one to three pips right of the zero line for a gain, left for a cost, and a bar on the zero line for no expected effect

specs.label: Uncertainty
specs.value: The atlas’s words, quoted; for a survey figure, its margin of error at the publisher’s stated confidence, 90 percent for the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, drawn as an interval

specs.label: A gap between two survey figures
specs.value: Counts only where it passes the margin of error of the gap itself; chapter 14 sets when a chart may rank survey figures

specs.label: Delay
specs.value: One, two or three ticks for under 2 years, 2 to 10 years and over 10 years, with the words

specs.label: Where a reform acts
specs.value: Its target connections in Rule 12.5’s red, at 4 px on a 1 px Charcoal edge and never at 2 px, with a note that names the reform

specs.label: Never
specs.value: A total across families, or a width or darkness for a grade

builders: Print each family’s code from the reform’s effects record with its qualifier, such as “+S delayed”, and write the families as Quality of democracy, Government efficacy, Economic performance, and Income and wealth equality.

rules.title: Write the source line in its six parts, in order.
rule: House rule H04 in chapter 02 sets the source line’s six parts and their order: the publisher, the title or table, the observation period, the geography, the date retrieved, and the qualification, the one caveat a reader most needs. The observation period is the time the numbers describe, and the date retrieved is the day we read the file. A chart prints the line under its notes, starting “Source:”, and a chart with two sources gives each its six parts.
A copy, a secondary source, an advocacy group and a value from our systems atlas each add a few words, which the Specifications set out.

text: A reader who doubts a number should be able to find it in a minute. The six parts in a fixed order tell them whose table to open, which rows, which years and places, and what the publisher says to watch for.

correct.caption: A jobs chart’s source line, taken apart into its parts, with the copy we read named after the geography. A line for a value from our systems atlas follows in the same order.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.6. The line names the database that copies the numbers and drops the publisher, the period, the date we read them and the warning that the last two months will change.

specs.label: Order
specs.value: Publisher, title or table, observation period, geography, date retrieved, qualification

specs.label: A copy
specs.value: The publisher first, then “via” and the copy’s name after the geography, such as FRED, the St. Louis Fed’s database

specs.label: A secondary source
specs.value: One that compiles other people’s records, with “a secondary source” after its name

specs.label: An advocacy group
specs.value: Named as one, as in “Unite America, an advocacy group”

specs.label: An atlas value
specs.value: Oath & Action’s systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, the record, snapshot of October 15, 2026

specs.label: Place
specs.value: Under the chart’s notes, in the caption style, starting “Source:”

builders: Print the line from the dataset’s own record, its printed source line, and never retype it, so the chart check can compare the two word for word.

rules.title: Print the period and the vintage, and give charts shown together one window.
rule: The measure line names the observation period, such as 2009 to 2025. Where a publisher revises its figures, the chart also names the vintage, the release its figures come from, and marks any figure the publisher calls preliminary. The Census Bureau’s release of September 15, 2026 carries corrected poverty thresholds for 2019 to 2024 and new weights for 2024, so a chart of those years names that release.

Charts shown together share one time window, printed once with its reason, and house rule H09 holds: “No chart or sentence splits a period at an inauguration date.” When a publisher revises a figure a published chart shows, the chart takes the new release and a dated update line that names it; a correction note (Rule 13.13) is for our own errors.

text: A reader who compares our chart with an older report may find another number for the same year and decide one of us made a mistake. The release named on the chart answers that before they ask, and one window lets a reader compare charts set side by side.
why.basis: Chapter 02, house rule H09, and the Census Bureau’s own revision notes

correct.caption: Two charts shown together in one window and on one scale, with the reason and the release named under them. The table shows the revision that makes the release matter.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.7. The title takes 2020 and 2021 from the earlier release and 2024 from the current one without naming either, and the chart beside it starts in another year.

specs.label: Period
specs.value: In the measure line, with months in words

specs.label: Vintage
specs.value: The release’s name and date, where the publisher revises its figures

specs.label: Preliminary figures
specs.value: Named in the qualification and marked on the chart

specs.label: One window
specs.value: The same first and last period and the same scale on every chart in a set, with its reason, printed once

specs.label: A publisher’s revision
specs.value: The new release, and an update line with its date and the release’s name

specs.label: Inauguration dates
specs.value: No chart or sentence splits a period at one (H09)

builders: Freeze each dataset with its release and the date we read it, and print both from that record. When a publisher revises, rebuild every chart in the set from the new release on one day, and name that release on each chart.

rules.title: Label an invented item Illustrative, beside the item.
rule: House rule H03 puts the word Illustrative beside every invented person, quote, place or figure a reader could take for real. A chart drawn from invented numbers carries “Illustrative data” beside its top edge, where a reader sees it before the numbers. When a piece mixes real and invented items, each invented item carries its own label and the real ones keep their sources. When every item in a piece is invented, one label at its head covers them all.

An invented bill takes a number from the ranges Rule 11.1 sets, from H.99001 and S.99002 up, which no legislature assigns, and an invented place takes a name we keep for examples, such as Alder County.

text: Many of our pieces set real and invented items side by side. A label beside each invented item tells a reader which is which at the moment they read it, while a note at the foot of a page arrives after they have believed what came before it.

correct.caption: A story card that mixes a real rule with an invented reader. The rule keeps its source, and the label sits beside the invented reader and her words.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.8. One note at the foot covers the card, so Ruth Okafor, an invented reader, and her words sit beside a real rule with nothing to set them apart.

specs.label: Beside the item
specs.value: Illustrative, in the label style, right after the invented name, quote, place or figure

specs.label: A chart
specs.value: “Illustrative data” beside its top edge

specs.label: Everything invented
specs.value: One label at the head of the piece

specs.label: Invented bills
specs.value: Numbers from Rule 11.1’s ranges

specs.label: Invented places
specs.value: Names kept for examples, such as Alder County

builders: Keep a flag on every invented item in a piece’s data and print the label from that flag, so a label cannot drift away from its item when the layout changes.

rules.title: Name every atlas ID in its typed chip.
rule: Our systems atlas gives each record a short ID, and some IDs repeat across kinds of record. The code B4 names both Variable B4 and Loop B4, B2, B3 and B5 repeat the same way, and Loop R1 sits one hyphen from Reform R-01. Every atlas ID we print sits in a typed chip, the outlined label that holds the kind of record and its ID together, such as Variable B4 or Loop B4, built as Rule 18.24 sets out. The first time a page names a record, its name follows the chip, as house rule H11 asks.

The kind word comes from the record’s place in the atlas, and the build checks every chip’s ID against the atlas before a page ships. In a source line, the kind word in plain text does the chip’s job, as in “connection L02”.

text: A bare B4 could mean hostility toward the other party or the loop in which electoral consequences can improve public performance, and the reader cannot tell which. The kind word settles it, and the chip keeps the word and the ID on one line.
why.basis: Chapter 02, house rule H11, and Rule 18.24

correct.caption: Three sentences that name records whose IDs collide, each ID in its chip with the record’s name after it.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.9. Bare codes leave the reader to guess that the first B4 is a variable and the second a loop, and that R1 and R-01 are different records.

specs.label: Chip
specs.value: The kind word and the ID in one outlined label, as Rule 18.24 builds it

specs.label: Kind words
specs.value: Variable, Connection, Loop, Reform, Issue, Claim, Domain, Route, Rule change and Delivery case

specs.label: In a source line
specs.value: The kind word in plain text before the ID, as in “connection L02” or “delivery case DL06”

specs.label: First use
specs.value: The record’s name after the chip

specs.label: The ID
specs.value: As the atlas writes it, with an ASCII hyphen, held on one line

specs.label: Check
specs.value: Every ID matched against the atlas before the page ships

builders: Write each chip from the record’s kind in the atlas, and let the build’s atlas check fail any chip whose ID the atlas does not hold.

rules.title: Date what can change, and print an undated route as not checked.
rule: A status, a count or a rule that can change after we publish carries the date it was last checked, in words, as in “as of October 15, 2026”. Our systems atlas dates its research as a snapshot, and its glossary defines one as “The dated state of the research behind the Atlas, most recently October 15, 2026.” Each fact the atlas rechecked also carries a date of its own. A page prints a fact’s own check date where it has one, and the snapshot date where it does not.

A route, one of the paths a reform can take to become law or practice, carries its check date when the atlas gives one and the words “Not checked” when it does not. Of the atlas’s 126 route entries, 13 carry a date. When something the record names has happened since its date, such as an election, the page keeps the dated words and adds what happened, with its own source and date.

text: A rating with no date reads as current, and a reader may act on it. “Not checked” tells them to look for themselves before they rely on the rating.
why.basis: Our systems atlas’s glossary entry “Snapshot” and its route records

correct.caption: Reform R-19’s three routes, each with its date: the atlas checked the federal route on October 15, 2026 and prints the other two as not checked. The status carries its own date.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.10. The heading says now and no route carries a date, so all three read as checked, though the atlas checked only one.

specs.label: A checked route
specs.value: “Checked” and the date, from the route’s own record

specs.label: An undated route
specs.value: “Not checked”, in the same type and place

specs.label: A status
specs.value: “As of” and the date, before the status words

specs.label: An atlas value
specs.value: “Snapshot of October 15, 2026” where it has no check date of its own

specs.label: Dates
specs.value: In words, as house rule H05 sets

builders: Print the check date from each route’s own record and “Not checked” where that field is empty, so a rating never borrows the reform’s status date.

rules.title: Draw documented events apart from causal claims.
rule: Our systems atlas keeps two logs of dated events. The repair log records 64 changes to the rules that decide who officials answer to, and the delivery log records 24 times government did something hard at scale with a measured result. An event records what happened on a date. A causal claim says that one thing moves another, and the atlas grades it.

On a chart or diagram, an event takes a mark of its own, a shape for its instrument with an outline for one still pending, and no arrowhead, line pattern or sign. Where the atlas codes an event’s direction, such as toward voters, the page prints the atlas’s words as the atlas’s assessment, with the atlas named, apart from the event’s date, place and text. A causal claim keeps the arrow, the sign and the line of Rule 13.4.

text: A ruling drawn as an arrow into a variable claims that the ruling moved the variable by an amount someone measured. The log records that the ruling happened and what it changed in the rules, and a mark of its own keeps a reader from taking it for more.
why.basis: Design judgment, from the atlas’s event mark our founder and editor approved in October 2026

correct.caption: Loop R1’s seven entries in the repair log, under the atlas’s own coding note, each a dated shape under a heading that says how the atlas codes it, then the loop’s three connections drawn as causal claims with their grades.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.11. A ruling drawn as a solid arrow with a plus sign reads as a measured effect on political spending, though the log records only that the ruling happened.

specs.label: Event shapes
specs.value: Ballot measure, a filled square; statute or local law, a wide bar; court ruling, a tall bar; executive or agency action, a framed square

specs.label: Pending
specs.value: The shape in outline

specs.label: Direction
specs.value: The atlas’s words, under a heading that names the atlas, such as “The atlas codes these rows toward voters”, with its coding note above the rows

specs.label: Left off
specs.value: Arrowheads, line patterns, signs and grade words on each event

specs.label: Label
specs.value: The date in words, the place and what the rule did, with the row’s ID in its chip

specs.label: Placement
specs.value: An event’s shape sits only at the head of its row, with the figure’s key, 6 px from its word; the record square sits only before the word Documented (Rule 13.4)

builders: Draw events from the logs’ rows and connections from the connection records, each with its own drawing function, so an event cannot pick up an arrowhead by a wrong flag.

rules.title: Quote a person exactly, with who, when and where.
rule: A quotation prints a person’s words exactly as the record holds them, set in Lora Italic as Rule 06.1 sets, and then says who said them, the role they held at the time, when, and where: the hearing, the ruling, the speech or the interview. A source line gives the record a reader can open. Words we add for sense sit in square brackets, and an ellipsis marks a cut only where the meaning stays the same.

In a chart or diagram, a quote sits beside the mark it speaks to as a note with its attribution, and the title stays our sentence about the evidence (Rule 13.1). An Act piece quotes each side at the same length (Rule 01.22), and an invented quote carries the Illustrative label beside it (Rule 13.8).

text: A quotation is the one place we print someone else’s words as theirs. The exact words with who, when and where let a reader check them, and they keep a famous paraphrase from passing for the original.

correct.caption: Justice Brandeis’s words as the Court’s opinion prints them, with his role, the case, the date and the record, set beside the atlas variable they speak to.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 13.12. The words in quotation marks appear nowhere in the opinion, and the line gives no role, date or place, so a reader cannot check them.

specs.label: The words
specs.value: Exactly as the record holds them, in Lora Italic, the opening mark hung (Rule 06.7)

specs.label: Who
specs.value: The name, and the role held at the time

specs.label: When and where
specs.value: The date in words, and the hearing, ruling, speech or interview

specs.label: Source
specs.value: A source line for the record a reader can open

specs.label: In a chart
specs.value: Beside the mark it speaks to, with its attribution, under a title that stays ours

specs.label: Added words
specs.value: In square brackets; a cut takes an ellipsis only where the meaning holds

builders: Copy a quotation from the record itself, never from an article that quotes it, and keep the record’s link in the piece’s notes.

rules.title: Correct in the open, with a dated note at the top.
rule: When a piece we published gets a fact, a figure or a chart wrong, we fix it and say so at its top. A correction note sits above the headline with the date of the fix and says what was wrong and what changed, in plain sentences. The fixed chart replaces the old one in the piece, so every reader and every share meets the right figures, and the note says what the old chart showed.

The same note goes on our corrections page, newest first, with the piece’s headline, a link to it and the date it first ran, and both stay as long as the piece is published. A correction takes no red: its words take the primary text color and its 4 px bar the essential graphic color, as Rule 26.3’s example sets out.

text: A note that says what was wrong lets a reader who saw the first version learn of the change, and anyone who shared the old figure can find out why it moved. Over months, the corrections page shows readers how often we get things wrong and how we fix it.
